planting.note: Plant container stock in spring near an established host shrub or tree, since quandong is hemiparasitic on neighboring root systems and establishes poorly without one; choose a lean, well-drained, full-sun arid-zone site.

directions: Plant in full sun on lean, sharply drained arid-zone soil, and site it within root-grafting distance of an established companion shrub or tree (acacia and casuarina species are commonly used), because quandong is a hemiparasitic tree that taps a host's roots for water and nutrients and establishes far more reliably with one nearby. Native to the dry inland of South Australia and commercially orcharded in the Flinders Ranges region, quandong produces bright red, tart fruits prized fresh and in the classic bush dessert quandong pie, as well as dried for preserves. Once established on a suitable host, it is extremely drought-tolerant and needs little supplemental water beyond occasional deep irrigation during fruit set.
sources: South Australian Research and Development Institute

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade; this species is distinct from the more widely known Queensland Davidson's plum (Davidsonia pruriens) and endemic to northern New South Wales rainforest.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade, protected from hot direct afternoon sun as a rainforest understory species. Davidsonia jerseyana, the Jersey or New South Wales type Davidson's plum, is a distinct species from the better-known Queensland Davidson's plum (Davidsonia pruriens), endemic to the rainforests of northern New South Wales and described as a separate species in the early 1990s. Like its Queensland relative it bears deep-purple, intensely tart plum-like fruit directly on the trunk and branches (cauliflory), grown commercially for the bushfood jam, sauce, and cordial trade. Give it steady moisture and rich, well-drained soil, and expect several years of growth before the first meaningful fruit set.
sources: Royal Botanic Garden Sydney — Australian Rainforest Plants

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Burdekin plum is dioecious, so plant both a male and a female tree if fruit is the goal.

directions: Plant in full sun on well-drained soil; Burdekin plum is heat- and drought-tolerant once established and native to open woodland of north Queensland. It belongs to the mango and cashew family (Anacardiaceae) and is dioecious, meaning individual trees are either male or female, so both sexes must be present for the female trees to set fruit. The purple-black, plum-like fruits are traditionally eaten fully ripe for their tart-sweet flavor, or lightly fermented, and have long been used by Aboriginal communities and in contemporary bushfood jams and jellies. Give young trees occasional water through their first dry season, after which they need very little irrigation.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, well-drained soil; young trees prefer part shade and benefit from a sheltered understory position before growing up toward the canopy.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in part shade while young, giving it a sheltered spot similar to its native rainforest understory habitat in northern New South Wales and southeast Queensland. Native tamarind is a large-leaved rainforest tree bearing clusters of tart, bright-orange fleshy pulp wrapped around large seeds, widely grown by bushfood producers for jams, sauces, and cordial. It grows into a substantial canopy tree over time, so allow ample room, and expect it to need consistent moisture through establishment rather than the drought tolerance of the dryland Australian bushfood species.
sources: Royal Botanic Garden Sydney — Australian Rainforest Plants

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, well-drained tropical soil in full sun to part shade; this north Queensland rainforest species is slower to establish than most bushfood trees, so budget for a longer wait to first fruit/nut set.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained tropical soil in full sun to part shade; Kuranda quandong is a north Queensland rainforest tree, unrelated to true quandong (Santalum), that produces a large, hard-shelled fruit whose kernel is roasted and eaten, sometimes informally called the Queensland chestnut. It is a true tropical species needing warm, humid, frost-free conditions year-round and is slower to establish and bear than most other Australian bushfood trees, so treat early fruiting-age estimates as approximate. Source from a specialty Australian native-plant nursery and give it a sheltered rainforest-edge position while young.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; creek lilly pilly adapts readily to hedge, screen, or specimen use along the east Australian coast and in similarly mild, humid climates.

directions: Plant in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; creek lilly pilly (now often reclassified as Syzygium smithii) is one of the most widely grown hedging and screening natives along Australia's east coast, valued for its dense evergreen foliage and tolerance of regular clipping. Its small pink-to-mauve berries are mildly tart-sweet and edible, traditionally used in jams and jellies, though the species is grown primarily as a landscape hedge or screen rather than a dedicated fruit crop. It tolerates both full sun and part shade and adapts to a range of moisture conditions once established, making it a versatile multi-purpose planting.
sources: Royal Botanic Garden Sydney — Australian Rainforest Plants
